1. Applicable legal framework  

- The claim is under the Part-time Workers (Prevention of Less Favourable Treatment) Regulations 2000 (“PTW Regulations”), implementing Council Directive 97/81/EC and its Framework Agreement on part-time work.
- Regulation 5(1) gives a part-time worker the right not to be treated less favourably than a comparable full‑time worker:
  - as regards contractual terms, or  
  - by being subjected to any other detriment.
- Regulation 5(2) limits that right to cases where:
  - (a) the treatment is “on the ground that the worker is a part-time worker”, and  
  - (b) the treatment is not justified on objective grounds.
- The Framework Agreement (clause 4(1)) provides that part-time workers shall not be treated in a less favourable manner than comparable full-time workers “solely because they work part time unless different treatment is justified on objective grounds”, and recognises the “pro rata temporis” principle.

So the court must address three main issues:
1. Was there less favourable treatment of a part-time worker compared with a full‑time comparator?  
2. If so, was that treatment “on the ground that” Reeves was part-time (and what degree of causation is required)?  
3. If yes to both, has Stone Rides shown that the treatment was justified on objective grounds?

---

2. Less favourable treatment  

(a) Existence of a comparator  

- The factual premise is that Reeves worked part-time as a driver and there were full‑time drivers doing the same job, using the same booking system. Those full‑time drivers are plainly “comparable full‑time workers” for Regulation 2(4)–(5) purposes.

(b) Nature of the alleged less favourable treatment  

- All drivers pay the same flat “circuit fee” to access the booking system.
- On its face the term is identical. However, anti‑discrimination law looks at substantive effect, not mere formal equality.
- The economic reality is that a fixed fee constitutes a larger proportion of a part‑time worker’s earnings than of a full‑time worker’s, because the cost cannot be spread over as many booked jobs/hours.

In the PTW context, the underlying principle (reflected in clause 4(2) of the Framework Agreement) is that, “where appropriate, the pro rata temporis principle shall apply.” That is, benefits and burdens attached to employment conditions should normally scale with working time, unless there is objective justification for a departure.

Here:

- A full‑timer can amortise the fee over a larger volume of work, so the net cost per booking or per hour is significantly lower than for a part‑timer.
- In substance, the part‑time driver is paying more for the same access, relative to the work they can perform, than the full‑time comparator.

A court is likely to characterise this as less favourable treatment of the part-time worker “as regards terms of his contract” (Reg 5(1)(a)) or, at the very least, as a detriment under Reg 5(1)(b), when viewed against the proper comparator and the pro rata temporis principle.

So the first limb (less favourable treatment vis‑à‑vis a full‑timer) is satisfied.

---

3. Causation: what does “on the ground that” require?  

This is the central legal issue in the fact pattern.

(a) The competing tests  

- Stone Rides argues for a “sole cause” test: Reeves must show that the only cause of the treatment was his part-time status; any concurrent objective such as revenue generation would defeat liability.
- Reeves argues for an “effective cause” (or substantial/operative cause) test: it is enough that part-time status was one real and effective reason for the treatment, even if other reasons existed.

(b) Text and purpose  

1. Domestic wording  

- Regulation 5(2)(a) uses “on the ground that the worker is a part-time worker”.
- Analogous discrimination provisions in UK law (e.g. “on racial grounds”, “on the ground of sex”, and under the Equality Act, “because of” a protected characteristic) have consistently been interpreted so that:
  - The protected characteristic need not be the sole or principal reason.
  - It is sufficient if it is an effective and operative cause of the treatment.

Cases such as Nagarajan v London Regional Transport [2000] 1 AC 501 confirm that where a prohibited ground is one effective cause of less favourable treatment, liability arises even if there are additional, non‑discriminatory reasons. That general approach to causation is now deeply embedded in the UK’s discrimination jurisprudence.

2. Directive and “solely because”  

- The Framework Agreement uses the phrase “solely because they work part time”.
- If that were read literally as requiring the worker to exclude any coexisting legitimate motive (profit, administrative simplicity, sector norms), protection would be virtually non‑existent: every employer can say, truthfully, that a policy is also motivated by commercial considerations.
- EU law and domestic courts interpret such expressions purposively. “Solely because” is used to distinguish treatment intrinsically linked to part-time status from treatment based on genuinely different, objective factors (e.g. different duties, different qualifications, or a separately justified operational requirement), not to allow an employer to rely on a general profit motive as a trump card.

Thus, to give practical effect to Directive 97/81, “on the ground that the worker is a part-time worker” must be interpreted in line with the established discrimination law standard: part-time status must be a real and effective cause of the treatment; it need not be the exclusive cause.

(c) Application to the facts  

The problem statement assumes that:

- “Both sides agree that his status as a part-time worker was a factor” in how he was treated.
- The disagreement is whether it must be the sole basis.

In other words, causation in fact is already conceded: Reeves’ part-time status played a real part in the way the fee structure bore upon him and other part‑timers.

Stone Rides’ profit/revenue rationale does not negate that:

- Profit-seeking or “revenue generation in line with sector norms” is a generic business motive; it does not explain why the particular structure chosen (a flat fee) was adopted, as opposed to a structure that would not place an extra burden on part‑timers (e.g. percentage commission, sliding scale, or pro‑rated fee).
- The disadvantage to part‑time workers is inseparable from their reduced hours; it is precisely because Reeves works part‑time that he bears a heavier burden. Thus his part‑time status is an effective cause of the less favourable treatment.

On a correct construction of the Regulations and Directive, Reeves does not have to prove that no other reason (such as profit) played any role. It is enough that his being part-time was an operative cause of the less favourable treatment. That test is satisfied on the assumed facts.

So, on the key point of statutory interpretation, the court should reject the “sole cause” test advanced by Stone Rides and adopt the “effective cause” test advanced by Reeves.

---

4. Objective justification  

Because part-time status is an effective ground of the less favourable treatment, the burden shifts to Stone Rides to show that the treatment is “justified on objective grounds” (Reg 5(2)(b)), mirroring an objective justification test similar to that used for indirect discrimination:

1. Legitimate aim  
   - Recovering the costs of running a booking system and generating revenue is a legitimate commercial aim. Aligning with sector norms and ensuring system sustainability are also capable of being legitimate objectives.

2. Appropriateness and necessity / proportionality  
   The crucial question is whether a flat, non‑pro‑rated fee, with its disproportionate impact on part‑timers, is a proportionate means of achieving those aims.

   Relevant considerations:

   - Less intrusive alternatives  
     - Stone Rides could charge a percentage commission on bookings, a fee scaled to usage, or a genuinely pro‑rated fee reflecting expected hours/turnover. Those models would recover costs and generate profit without imposing a relatively heavier burden on part‑time drivers.
   - Severity of disadvantage  
     - For a part‑time driver, the fee consumes a significantly larger proportion of income and may make participation uneconomic. For a full‑time driver, the same fee may be easily absorbed. That degree of relative disadvantage is substantial rather than marginal.
   - Administrative convenience and “sector norms”  
     - While ease of administration and conformity with industry practice are relevant, they are not, in themselves, strong enough justification to maintain a model that imposes systematic relative disadvantage on a protected class of workers where less discriminatory alternatives are readily available.
   - The pro rata temporis principle  
     - The underlying EU principle is that employment-related advantages and burdens should ordinarily be proportionate to working time. Departures require specific, weighty justification. A flat fee that is inherently non‑pro‑rated and hits part‑timers hardest runs against that norm.

On these facts, Stone Rides’ justification case is weak. The company has:

- A legitimate aim, but
- Chosen a method (flat fee) that is plainly more burdensome for part‑timers and
- Not shown that it is necessary or that less discriminatory alternatives would seriously undermine the business objective.

A court applying orthodox proportionality analysis is likely to conclude that Stone Rides has not discharged the burden of showing “objective justification”.

---

5. Overall conclusion  

Step by step:

1. Reeves is a part‑time worker with full‑time comparators.  
2. The flat circuit fee constitutes less favourable treatment in substance, viewed through the pro rata temporis lens.  
3. His part‑time status is an effective cause of that disadvantage; UK and EU law do not require it to be the sole cause. “Sole cause” as argued by Stone Rides would seriously undermine the protective purpose of the Directive and Regulations.  
4. Stone Rides’ justifications (revenue, sector norms, uniformity) are legitimate aims but the flat, non‑pro‑rated fee is not a proportionate means of achieving them, given its particular and predictable burden on part‑time workers and the availability of less discriminatory charging structures.

Accordingly, on a proper interpretation of the PTW Regulations 2000 and Directive 97/81, Avalon Reeves should succeed.

The claim turns on two linked questions:

1. Did Iris House belong beneficially to Jade Energy Ventures at the time of the impugned transfer, so that its disposal could be a “transaction at an undervalue” under s 423 Insolvency Act 1986?  
2. Or was Jade already holding Iris House on trust for Emerald Pension Fund under a trust that satisfies s 53(1)(b) Law of Property Act 1925, so that transferring the legal title to Emerald did not deplete Jade’s assets?

If Jade was only ever a bare trustee, then in substance there was no asset of Jade’s for Steel Horizon to be deprived of.

I will address:

- A. The legal test under s 423 IA 1986  
- B. The effect of property being held on trust  
- C. Whether there was a valid, evidenced trust under s 53(1)(b) LPA 1925  
- D. Application to these facts and who should prevail  

---

### A. Section 423 Insolvency Act 1986

Section 423 requires:

1. **A “transaction” at an undervalue** – broadly, a gift or a disposition where the debtor receives no consideration or consideration significantly less than the value of the property (s 423(1), (1)(a)–(c)).  
2. **A “purpose” requirement** – the debtor must have entered into the transaction for the purpose (or one of the purposes) of putting assets beyond the reach of creditors or otherwise prejudicing their interests (s 423(3)).

Crucially, s 423 operates on **property of the debtor**. If what is transferred is not, in substance, an asset of the debtor but trust property held for someone else, then there is no depletion of the debtor’s estate in the relevant sense.

So the prior issue is: **what interest, if any, did Jade beneficially own in Iris House?**

---

### B. Effect of trust ownership on the s 423 analysis

Basic principles of English trust and insolvency law:

- Where A holds legal title to land **on trust** for B,  
  - A’s beneficial interest is either non-existent (bare trustee) or limited.  
  - The **trust assets are not available to A’s general creditors**. On A’s insolvency they are treated as trust property, not part of the insolvent estate; the insolvency office-holder takes subject to the trust.

Therefore:

- If Jade held Iris House **beneficially**, its transfer to Emerald could clearly be a transfer of Jade’s asset, capable of challenge under s 423.  
- If Jade held Iris House **on trust** for Emerald, and merely transferred the legal title to Emerald as beneficiary:
  - Jade divested itself only of bare legal title, which has negligible economic value and would not (in any real sense) have been available to Jade’s creditors anyway.  
  - Moreover, satisfying an existing obligation to convey legal title to the true beneficiary is not normally characterised as an “undervalue”: the “consideration” is discharge of that pre‑existing equitable obligation, which is equivalent in value to the legal estate being transferred.

So Steel Horizon can only succeed if it shows that **no valid trust existed**, so that Iris House was genuinely part of Jade’s own asset base.

That turns on **s 53(1)(b) LPA 1925**.

---

### C. Was there a valid, properly evidenced trust under s 53(1)(b) LPA 1925?

#### 1. The statutory requirement

Section 53(1)(b) states:

> “a declaration of trust respecting any land or any interest therein must be manifested and proved by some writing signed by **some person who is able to declare such trust** or by his will.”

Key points:

- The provision is **evidentiary, not constitutive**. An express trust of land can be created orally; s 53(1)(b) requires that it be “manifested and proved” by signed writing before a court will enforce it.  
- The writing:
  - need not be the original declaration of trust;  
  - can be created **after** the trust has arisen;  
  - can be any document that clearly acknowledges the trust and identifies property, trustee and beneficiary.
- The “person who is able to declare such trust” is the person(s) who own the legal estate or otherwise have the power to create the trust. For a company, that person is the company itself, acting through its authorised signatories.

Courts have repeatedly accepted that **subsequent documents** can satisfy s 53(1)(b) provided they sufficiently evidence the trust (e.g. cases like *Rochefoucauld v Boustead* applied by analogy; also the general line of authority that later acknowledgments can manifest and prove the trust).

#### 2. Can the mortgage documents serve as the required writing?

On the facts:

- Two **mortgage-related documents** were signed by representatives of Jade Energy Ventures.  
- Jade says these documents “showed that Emerald Pension Fund was the genuine beneficial owner of Iris House” and that filing them “confirmed an existing trust relationship.”

This is significant because:

- They are in writing.  
- They are signed by persons acting for Jade, the legal owner.  
- Their content (as described) expressly acknowledges that the beneficial ownership lies with Emerald.

Nothing in s 53(1)(b) requires:

- That the document be labelled “Declaration of Trust”.  
- That it be executed for the **primary** purpose of constituting a trust.  
- That it be separate from commercial documentation such as mortgage instruments.

What matters is whether the documents, viewed objectively, **manifest and prove** that Jade holds the property on trust for Emerald.

If the mortgage instruments, in the usual way, recite or acknowledge that Jade is holding as trustee or that Emerald is the beneficial owner, that is very likely sufficient:

- They clearly identify the land (Iris House),  
- identify Jade as legal owner,  
- identify Emerald as beneficial owner, and  
- are signed by persons authorised to act for Jade.

Courts routinely treat such acknowledgments as satisfying s 53(1)(b). The statute’s purpose is to prevent fraud and evidential uncertainty, not to impose a hyper‑technical form of document drafting.

#### 3. Does it matter that the signatories were “representatives” rather than Jade itself?

Steel Horizon’s point is that:

- s 53(1)(b) allows writing signed by “some person who is able to declare such trust”, and  
- unlike s 53(1)(a) and (c), it does not expressly mention an “agent”,  
- therefore, they say, an agent’s signature is insufficient and the landowner itself must sign.

There are several problems with that argument on these facts.

1. **A company can only act through human agents.**  
   Where company officers or authorised signatories execute a document on the company’s behalf, they are treated in law as the company’s signature, not as some independent “stranger” whose acts do not bind the company.

2. The statutory language “some person who is able to declare such trust” is naturally read to include the legal owner acting through its usual corporate machinery. There is no realistic policy reason to distinguish between:
   - a director signing a mortgage (with an embedded trust acknowledgment), and  
   - the same director signing a stand‑alone “Declaration of Trust” – yet Steel’s construction would validate the latter but not the former.

3. Even if one drew a conceptual line between principal and “agent”, **the reality of corporate execution** is that authorised signatories are the means by which the company, as owner, signs; their signature counts as the company’s signature for property and contract law purposes.

4. The courts are slow to let s 53(1)(b) be used **as an instrument of fraud**. A trustee (and persons claiming through them, such as creditors) is not allowed to rely on technical non-compliance to defeat a genuine trust arrangement where there is clear written evidence. That policy, evident in decisions like *Rochefoucauld v Boustead* and its progeny, strongly favours treating these signed mortgage documents as adequate manifestation of the trust.

On the facts as given, there is no suggestion that the people signing the mortgage documents lacked authority to bind Jade in relation to Iris House. If they had authority to mortgage the property, it is difficult to argue they lacked authority to state the basis (trustee/beneficial ownership) on which Jade held it.

#### 4. Foreign law “arrangement” and timing

Jade’s story is that:

- Iris House beneficially belonged to Emerald from the outset under some arrangement governed by foreign law;  
- and, if required by English law because the land is in England, Jade declared a trust for Emerald’s benefit, evidenced by the mortgage documents.

Two points:

1. **Lex situs**: The creation of proprietary interests in English land is governed by English law. Whatever the content of the foreign-law arrangement, as regards title to Iris House the English court will ask whether the ingredients of an English trust are made out. The foreign arrangement is relevant primarily as evidence of intention.

2. **Timing**: If the arrangement and/or trust existed **long before** Steel Horizon’s arbitral award and enforcement, that significantly undercuts any suggestion that the trust is a late, “convenient” device to avoid Steel’s claim. The fact that the trust is recorded in earlier, independent mortgage documents is particularly powerful: those documents are generated for dealings with a third-party lender, not for the purpose of this litigation.

Even if Jade’s explanation has “shifted” (foreign arrangement first, then trust “if needed”), courts primarily look to **objective documentary evidence**, not litigation gloss. If the mortgage documents pre‑date the enforcement action and clearly acknowledge Emerald as beneficial owner, they are cogent evidence that Jade has long regarded Iris House as held for Emerald.

---

### D. Application: was there a s 423 transaction at an undervalue?

Putting these strands together:

1. **Existence of a trust**  
   - There appears to be a longstanding arrangement under which Emerald was the beneficial owner.  
   - That arrangement is “manifested and proved” by two mortgage-related documents:
     - in writing,  
     - signed on behalf of Jade as legal owner,  
     - expressly acknowledging Emerald as beneficial owner.
   - Those documents satisfy s 53(1)(b). The trust is therefore valid and enforceable in equity. 

2. **What interest did Jade own?**  
   - Once the trust is recognised, Jade’s interest in Iris House is at most a **bare legal estate**, subject to the obligation to hold it and ultimately convey it to Emerald.  
   - That bare legal title is **not an asset available to Jade’s general creditors** in any meaningful sense; on insolvency, the office-holder would hold Iris House on the same trust for Emerald.

3. **Effect of the transfer to Emerald**  
   - The subsequent transfer of Iris House to Emerald Pension Fund is simply the vesting of legal title in the already existing beneficial owner.  
   - Economically, Jade gives up no real value of its own; it merely performs its pre-existing equitable obligation as trustee.  
   - Thus, the transfer is not a “transaction at an undervalue” as regards Jade’s estate: the consideration is the discharge of Jade’s trustee obligations, which is commensurate with the value of what is transferred.

4. **Purpose under s 423**  
   - The suspicious timing (shortly after Steel obtained permission to enforce the award) would be highly significant **if** Iris House were truly Jade’s own asset.  
   - But if Jade and Emerald had already arranged – and documented – that Emerald was the beneficial owner, Jade’s purpose in aligning legal with beneficial title is better characterised as:
     - performing trust obligations and regularising the position;  
     - protecting Emerald’s existing property from being wrongly treated as Jade’s asset.  
   - Section 423 is aimed at debtors stripping assets that genuinely belong to them; it is not intended to allow creditors to annex third parties’ trust property merely because the timing of formal transfer is awkward.

5. **Steel Horizon’s reliance on s 53(1)(b)**  
   - Creditors such as Steel stand in the shoes of the debtor and cannot obtain better rights to the property than the debtor had.  
   - If, as against Emerald, Jade could not honestly deny the trust (given the signed mortgage documents and long‑standing arrangement), then Steel cannot use s 53(1)(b) as a technical escape route to expand Jade’s beneficial interest.  
   - Allowing Steel to defeat Emerald’s trust on the basis of a strained reading of s 53(1)(b) would risk using the statute *as an instrument of fraud*, contrary to the equitable principle underlying the provision.

Given the factual matrix as presented – especially the prior, independent mortgage documents acknowledging Emerald as beneficial owner – an English court, applying orthodox trust and insolvency principles, is more likely to find that:

- Iris House was **already held on trust** for Emerald Pension Fund in a manner that satisfies s 53(1)(b);  
- Jade’s beneficial interest was negligible or non‑existent; and therefore  
- the transfer of legal title to Emerald was **not** a transaction at an undervalue under s 423 IA 1986.

Accordingly, Steel Horizon’s s 423 claim should fail, and Jade Energy Ventures should prevail.

1. **Statutory framework**

- Before the Building Safety Act 2022 (BSA), ShelterCo’s rights to recover via service charge were governed by:
  - the leases; and
  - the Landlord and Tenant Act 1985 (particularly s.19 on reasonableness and s.27A on “payability” of service charges).

- The BSA 2022, in particular **Schedule 8**, creates a *superimposed* regime for “relevant buildings” and “qualifying leases” which:
  - limits or excludes service charge recovery for **“relevant defects”**; and  
  - expressly bars recovery of certain **legal and professional costs** via service charge (Sch 8, para 9).

The dispute is essentially whether those Schedule 8 protections apply to **costs incurred before the BSA provisions came into force**, or whether they bite only on *post‑commencement* expenditure.

---

2. **Is Lowbridge Towers within the BSA leaseholder protections?**

On the stated facts:

- The building is over 18m tall → it is a **“relevant building”** for BSA purposes.
- The 32 flats are held on long leases of dwellings → they are on the face of it **qualifying leases** (subject to detailed statutory conditions, but none are said to be absent).
- The defects are fire safety issues in the external wall construction → these are classic candidates for **“relevant defects”** within Sch 8 (defects in design, construction or materials creating a building safety risk arising from works done before 28 June 2022).

So the statutory protections in **Schedule 8** are, in principle, engaged.

---

3. **What does Schedule 8 actually regulate?**

Schedule 8 does not purport to rewrite the leases; it **regulates what service charge is “payable”** under qualifying leases in respect of:

- the costs of **remedying relevant defects** (“relevant measures”); and
- certain associated legal/professional costs (para 9).

The key point is linguistic: the focus is on **“payability”** of service charges. That is exactly the same concept used in s.27A of the 1985 Act, under which tribunals determine “whether a service charge is payable” and, if so, how much.  

Schedule 8 overlays that pre‑existing framework by declaring that, in certain circumstances, **“no service charge is payable”** (or only a capped amount is payable) even if the lease, read alone, would have allowed recovery.

Accordingly:

- ShelterCo may well have **contractual provisions** entitling it, in general terms, to recover repair/compliance costs, and
- those provisions are still “valid” in the abstract;
- but the **statute now controls whether and to what extent they can be enforced**.

That is a typical and orthodox way in which later statutes interact with existing contracts in landlord and tenant law.

---

4. **Retroactivity: how far back do the Schedule 8 protections reach?**

ShelterCo’s core contention is that because many costs were *incurred* before the BSA came into force, a reading which deprives it of recovery would be impermissibly retrospective.

(a) **Presumption against retroactivity**

There is indeed a strong presumption that Parliament does not intend to:

- take away vested rights; or
- impose new liabilities;

in relation to **completed events** in the past, absent clear words or necessary implication.

However:

- That is a **presumption**, not a rule of law.
- It yields where the statutory language and structure show Parliament intended the legislation to bear on past facts.

Crucially, there is a recognised distinction between:

- changing the **legal consequences of acts already completed and obligations already fully crystallised** (true retroactivity), and
- changing the **legal position for the future in relation to existing relationships** (e.g. leases), even though that inevitably affects expectations based on past arrangements.

The BSA plainly falls into the latter category.

(b) **The wording and structure of Schedule 8**

Several features show that Schedule 8 is intended to address **historic building safety defects** and their financial consequences:

1. A “relevant defect” is, by definition, one arising from **things done before a cut‑off date** (before 28 June 2022). That makes sense only if the protections are aimed squarely at long‑standing problems, not just future works.

2. The operative provisions are framed in terms of **whether a service charge is payable**, without any limitation to costs incurred after commencement. Parliament could easily have confined them to costs incurred after a certain date; it did not.

3. The evident legislative purpose – expressly and repeatedly stated in the political and policy context – is to shift the burden of historic remediation away from residential leaseholders. If the protections applied only to *future* expenditure, landlords could simply do works early and demand payment before the Act came into force, undermining that purpose entirely.

In other words, the statute is deliberately addressing the financial consequences of **pre‑existing defects**. To give effect to that purpose, it must necessarily affect **future service charge demands** raised *after* commencement, even where the underlying works or costs were prior.

This is a classic example of change in the law governing **future enforcement** of pre‑existing contractual mechanisms – not a retrospective rewriting of history.

(c) **Accrued contractual rights vs statutory limits on enforcement**

Even if ShelterCo’s contractual right to recoup costs arises when it incurs them, that does not guarantee that any particular **sum is enforceable in court** thereafter. Parliament routinely imposes new limits on enforcement of service charge clauses (e.g. through reasonableness requirements, consultation rules, limitation periods, or new kinds of prohibition). Those later statutes:

- apply to **ongoing and future payment disputes**; and
- may bar or reduce recovery of costs already incurred,  
  without being treated as impermissibly retrospective.

The BSA fits that model: it does not undo payments already made, nor does it invalidate the leases; it governs what ShelterCo may now lawfully recover from leaseholders going forward.

---

5. **Effect on the different categories of cost here**

(a) **Fire safety remedial and interim measures (pre‑commencement)**

These are plainly “relevant measures” taken (or to be taken) in relation to “relevant defects” in a relevant building.

Given the above:

- Any service charge demands **made or determined now** fall to be tested **against Schedule 8**, regardless of when the underlying cost was incurred.
- That regime may:
  - **completely prohibit** recovery for some categories of defect (e.g. where landlord or an associated party is responsible under the Act – a factual question not fully specified here); or
  - **cap** the aggregate total recoverable from each qualifying leaseholder (e.g. the monetary caps for London); and
  - prevent recovery where the leaseholder meets specified low‑value or hardship thresholds.

The question posed is binary – “whether, and to what extent, the BSA restricts ShelterCo from recovering pre‑commencement costs”. On the facts given, the correct analysis is:

- The BSA **does restrict** ShelterCo’s ability to recover *pre‑commencement* remediation and fire safety costs through service charges, though it **may permit partial recovery** within the statutory caps if the detailed conditions are satisfied.
- ShelterCo cannot rely on the leases and the 1985 Act alone to recover all of those costs; the BSA is a subsequent, more specific statute that prevails over general contractual and earlier statutory rights in case of conflict.

(b) **Legal and professional costs for enforcing recovery**

Schedule 8, paragraph 9, is particularly clear. In substance, it provides that:

- **no service charge is payable** under a qualifying lease in respect of **legal or other professional services** relating to:
  - liability (or potential liability) under the BSA in relation to relevant defects; or
  - liability (or potential liability) of any person as a result of a relevant defect.

ShelterCo’s “legal steps to ensure it could bill those expenses through service charges” fall squarely within that description:

- They relate directly to its potential liability and its attempts to pass costs on for relevant defects.
- Paragraph 9 is framed in absolute terms: **no such costs are recoverable via service charge**, and it is not qualified by when those costs were incurred.

Accordingly, even if some remedial costs could still be recovered (subject to BSA caps and conditions), ShelterCo **cannot recover its legal and related professional costs** of fighting this issue through the service charge.

---

6. **ShelterCo’s equity/fairness arguments**

ShelterCo raises policy and fairness concerns:

- It relied on service charge provisions and minimal ground rent;
- It acted in good faith to address serious fire safety defects;
- Denying recovery allegedly creates perverse incentives for freeholders.

Those points carry some moral weight, but they cannot override a clear statutory scheme. Moreover:

- The **entire object** of the leaseholder protections is to reallocate the risk of historical building safety defects **away from leaseholders** and towards:
  - developers, associated landlords, and
  - more broadly, freeholders and the industry.
- Parliament simultaneously created mechanisms such as **Remediation Orders and Remediation Contribution Orders** to ensure landlords and others **do** remediate and can, where appropriate, recover from responsible parties rather than from occupiers.

So although ShelterCo’s position is understandable, the Court’s role is to give **effect** to Parliament’s chosen allocation of risk, not to restore the previous contractual balance under the guise of avoiding retrospectivity.

---

7. **Interaction with the Landlord and Tenant Act 1985**

The 1985 Act established a general regime for service charges but is not an entrenched code. Later legislation can – and often does – qualify or displace it.

Here:

- Where Schedule 8 says “no service charge is payable” or imposes caps and conditions, that is **determinative** of payability under s.27A of the 1985 Act.
- Any broader contractual right in the leases, or more generous recoverability under the 1985 Act alone, is **cut down** by the specific, later BSA provisions.

Thus, the Occupants are correct that ShelterCo cannot use the 1985 Act to “bypass” the BSA protections.

---

8. **Conclusion**

An English court, applying orthodox principles of statutory interpretation and giving due weight to the structure and purpose of Schedule 8, should conclude:

- The Building Safety Act 2022 **does** restrict ShelterCo’s ability to recover **pre‑commencement** remediation and fire safety costs via service charges, because the question is whether those costs are **payable now**, and Schedule 8 is expressly aimed at historic “relevant defects”.
- The landlord’s contractual and 1985 Act rights are **subordinated** to the later, more specific statutory protections.
- In any event, Schedule 8 paragraph 9 clearly and absolutely **bars recovery of the legal and professional costs** incurred in relation to liability for relevant defects and the leaseholder protections.

On that analysis, the Occupants’ position aligns more closely with the statute, and they should prevail on the central issue of service charge liability for the disputed pre‑commencement costs (subject only to any limited recovery that may remain available within the BSA’s statutory caps and conditions).

1. **Which execution date controls? 1971 or 1982?**

a. **Role of state wills law and codicils**

For federal estate tax, the nature and timing of property interests are determined by state law. Under classic wills doctrine, a codicil “republishes” a will as of the date of the codicil, meaning that—absent a contrary statute or very specific context—the will is treated as having been executed on the date of the last codicil.

Nothing in the facts suggests that the relevant state has rejected this doctrine; to the contrary, the summary “under settled principles of wills law” is correct: a later codicil that modifies dispositive provisions generally re‑executes the entire will as of the codicil’s date.

Here, Mary Winston did not merely correct scrivener’s errors or change an executor; her codicils “adjusted some details regarding Kevin Fletcher’s lifetime benefits.” That is a substantive change to a *beneficial interest* under the trust. Under ordinary republication-by‑codicil doctrine, that is enough to cause the testamentary scheme to be treated as executed as of the latest codicil—1982.

b. **Interaction with the federal cutoff for “more permissive rules”**

The tax problem, by hypothesis, is that:

- Instruments “executed” **before** a statutory cutoff date (here, the regime invoked by Harper Bank for the 1971 will) are governed by more permissive split‑interest rules, while  
- Instruments “executed” **after** that cutoff (here, 1982) are subject to the stricter requirement that a charitable remainder follow a CRAT/CRUT‑type interest or otherwise be presently ascertainable under more demanding standards.

Congress typically uses execution‑date cutoffs precisely to avoid indefinite grandfathering of arrangements that taxpayers continue to modify over time. When a testator reviews and amends the dispositive provisions in 1982, the reliance interest justifying grandfathering largely disappears. That policy cuts against Harper Bank’s position.

c. **Harper’s “minor adjustment” argument**

Harper Bank argues that the “core charitable scheme” did not change; only Kevin Fletcher’s benefits were adjusted. But federal transition provisions normally look to:

- The execution date of the *governing instrument*, not a segmented “charitable portion,” and
- Whether the changes are substantive in economic effect, not merely whether the charitable remainderman’s nominal identity stayed the same.

Changing the amount or character of the life tenant’s benefits is itself economically substantive; it changes the expected value of the noncharitable interest and correspondingly the value of the charitable remainder.

On these facts, a court applying standard wills principles and federal transition rules would treat the Winston will as **executed in 1982**, not 1971. That places the trust squarely under the post‑cutoff, stricter split‑interest rules.

2. **Does the unreformed trust qualify under the post‑cutoff rules?**

Assuming 1982 controls, we then ask whether, as of Mary’s death in 1985, the remainder to Elmwood University is deductible.

a. **Post‑cutoff requirements**

For a charitable remainder following a noncharitable interest, the 1969 reforms (and later elaborations) impose two core constraints:

1. The interest must be in a statutorily prescribed form (e.g., a charitable remainder annuity trust or unitrust, or certain pooled income funds), *or*  
2. If not in those exact forms, the charitable remainder must still be “presently ascertainable” and “severable” from the noncharitable interest at the date of death, so its value can be reliably determined.

In practice, once the post‑cutoff rules apply, the IRS and regulations are quite rigid: a remainder following a flexible, discretionary, consumption‑based life interest typically does *not* qualify.

b. **Nature of Kevin Fletcher’s original interest**

Kevin Fletcher’s interest as created by the will and codicils consisted of:

- Specified monthly financial payments, **plus**
- Payment of “medical expenses, taxes, upkeep and improvements” on a Riverside residence, **plus**
- “Other expenditures” of a similar open-ended character.

The key features:

- The trustee has broad authority to expend principal on Fletcher’s behalf.  
- The obligation for “upkeep and improvements” and “other expenditures” is not cabined by an objective, external standard that limits the extent of corpus invasion. “Improvements” in particular can expand drastically in scope (e.g., expensive remodeling, additions, luxury upgrades), and “other expenditures” is, as described, open‑ended.

This looks less like a fixed income interest and more like a life estate coupled with a discretionary spending power that, in economic substance, could exhaust the corpus.

c. **Presently ascertainable value of the charitable remainder**

Even before the 1969 Act, the Supreme Court and the Treasury made clear that a charitable remainder is deductible only where its value is “presently ascertainable” at the decedent’s death. Where a trustee may invade principal for a noncharitable beneficiary without a clearly measurable, external standard (e.g., “for comfort, happiness, welfare”), courts routinely hold that the charitable remainder is too uncertain to value and therefore no deduction is allowed.

Here:

- Some components are measurable (e.g., routine taxes and basic upkeep).  
- But the *right* to “improvements” and “other expenditures” is not subject to a tight, objective limit or formula. A trustee could approve major and repeated capital improvements, or generous discretionary spending, significantly eroding or eliminating the corpus.

Because those discretionary powers are not bounded by a clearly defined, actuarially manageable standard, it is not possible, as of 1985, to compute with reasonable certainty how much principal must remain for Elmwood University. That makes the charitable remainder’s value **not presently ascertainable** in the sense required for § 2055.

Thus, under the post‑cutoff regime (which applies if the instrument is deemed executed in 1982), the original arrangement **does not qualify** for a charitable deduction.

3. **Can the 1988 reformation rescue the deduction under § 2055(e)(3)?**

a. **Purpose and limits of § 2055(e)(3)**

Section 2055(e)(3) was enacted to *mitigate the harshness* of the split‑interest rules when a decedent’s instrument clearly intended a charitable remainder but failed to adopt the precise statutory forms. It allows a post‑death judicial “qualified reformation” which, if it meets the statutory conditions:

- Revises the noncharitable and charitable interests into compliant forms (e.g., a CRAT or CRUT), and  
- Causes the charitable remainder to be treated for tax purposes as if it had been created in the qualified form from the outset.

But Congress cabin\xaded this relief carefully. For an interest to be “reformable” and for a reformation to be “qualified,” the statute and implementing regulations require, among other things:

- That the pre‑ and post‑reformation interests be **economically very close**—the actuarial value of the new interest to the noncharitable beneficiary cannot differ from the old interest’s value by more than a small tolerance (commonly described as a 5% limit).  
- That the reformation not create, in substance, a *new* and significantly different economic arrangement.

These limits were designed to prevent taxpayers from using § 2055(e)(3) to rewrite dispositive schemes after death in order to obtain tax benefits that do not correspond to the decedent’s original economic intent.

b. **Nature of the 1988 reformation**

The 1988 state-court decree converted Fletcher’s interest from:

- A combination of monthly payments and **broad, open‑ended rights** to expenditures (including potentially unlimited “improvements” and other expenses) funded from the trust,

into:

- A **fixed annual amount**—a classic annuity‑type payment.

Economically, this is a major shift:

- Before reformation, Fletcher could, in principle, receive quite large benefits in kind and in cash, constrained primarily by trustee discretion, not by a fixed formula.  
- After reformation, his benefits are strictly limited to a fixed sum each year—removing his previous ability (through the trustee) to deplete the corpus for improvements and other discretionary expenditures.

The actuarial value of a fixed annuity calculated at Fletcher’s age in 1985 is highly unlikely to approximate, within a 5% band, the actuarial value of a life interest that includes both guaranteed payments and potentially unlimited capital improvements and discretionary spending. The discretionary consumption component is precisely what made the original remainder unascertainable.

As a result, the 1988 decree is not a minor technical correction; it is a **substantive rewrite** of the economic rights of the life beneficiary.

c. **Effect under § 2055(e)(3) and federal tax law**

Given the magnitude of this change:

- The original noncharitable interest is not a “reformable interest” within the meaning of § 2055(e)(3), because the post‑reformation annuity interest is too different in value and structure from the pre‑reformation discretionary consumption interest.  
- The reformation therefore is not a “qualified reformation”; it fails the statutory conditions designed to maintain rough economic equivalence.

Moreover, under *Commissioner v. Estate of Bosch*, federal courts are not obliged to accept a lower state‑court reformation as dispositive of property interests for federal tax purposes, especially where it appears primarily tax‑motivated. They instead determine independently, using the best evidence of state law and federal statutory purpose, whether such a reformation should be given retroactive effect for federal tax.

On these facts, a federal court would almost certainly conclude that the 1988 decree cannot be treated as retroactively converting the original discretionary life interest into a qualifying CRAT‑like annuity for § 2055 purposes.

Accordingly, § 2055(e)(3) does **not** save the deduction.

4. **Does Mary Winston’s clear charitable intent change the result?**

Mary Winston’s charitable intent toward Elmwood University is obvious and consistent over many years. But for federal estate tax:

- Charitable deductions are a matter of **legislative grace**; taxpayers must meet the specific statutory conditions.  
- The Supreme Court has repeatedly held that good motive or charitable aspiration cannot substitute for compliance with technical requirements.

Here:

- The trust, as actually written and in force at death, gave Kevin Fletcher a non‑CRAT/CRUT, open‑ended discretionary interest that made the charitable remainder’s value unascertainable.  
- The subsequent reformation substantially altered that interest and does not fit within the tightly constrained relief allowed by § 2055(e)(3).  

Denying the deduction is not a judgment on Winston’s philanthropy; it is an application of the conditions Congress placed on access to the charitable estate tax deduction after the 1969 reforms.

5. **Summary**

- Under standard wills doctrine, Winston’s 1982 codicil republishes and re‑executes the will as of 1982, placing the trust under the stricter post‑cutoff split‑interest rules.  
- Under those rules, the original trust’s provisions—broad, open‑ended authority to spend for Fletcher’s benefit, including “improvements” and “other expenditures”—make the value of Elmwood University’s remainder not presently ascertainable and thus not deductible.  
- The 1988 state‑court reformation converts Fletcher’s interest into a fixed annuity, fundamentally changing its economic character. That change is too great to qualify as a “qualified reformation” under § 2055(e)(3); the statute does not permit such a retroactive rewrite for federal tax purposes.  
- Charitable intent, however admirable, cannot overcome these statutory and regulatory barriers.

On this analysis, a U.S. court should rule that the estate is **not** entitled to an estate tax charitable deduction for the remainder to Elmwood University.

1. Statutory and EU framework  

- Part-time Workers (Prevention of Less Favourable Treatment) Regulations 2000 (“PTW Regs”), reg 5:  
  - A part‑time worker has the right not to be treated less favourably than a comparable full‑time worker as regards terms of contract or any other detriment.  
  - That right applies only if:  
    (a) “the treatment is on the ground that the worker is a part‑time worker”, and  
    (b) the treatment is not justified on objective grounds.

- The PTW Regs implement Clause 4 of the Framework Agreement on part‑time work (Directive 97/81/EC), which provides:  
  “In respect of employment conditions, part-time workers shall not be treated in a less favourable manner than comparable full‑time workers solely because they work part time unless different treatment is justified on objective grounds.”

The UK court must interpret reg 5 compatibly with Clause 4 and with general EU and domestic discrimination principles.

---

2. What does “on the ground that” require?  

(a) Mixed‑motive discrimination in general discrimination law  

UK discrimination law has consistently rejected a “sole reason” test:

- In *Nagarajan v London Regional Transport* [1999] IRLR 572 (HL), concerning race discrimination, the House of Lords held that discrimination occurs where the protected ground is an effective cause, or has a significant influence, on the treatment. It need not be the only or even the main reason.  
- Similar formulations (“a significant influence”, “a material and effective cause”) are used throughout discrimination case law, including under the Equality Act 2010.

The phrase “on grounds of” or “on the ground that” has been treated as requiring a causal connection, not exclusivity of motive.

(b) Consistency with Directive 97/81  

Clause 4 speaks of less favourable treatment “solely because” the worker is part‑time, but then immediately allows different treatment if “justified on objective grounds”.

If “solely because” were read as a strict “sole motive” test, employers could almost always escape liability by pointing to some additional commercial motive such as cost‑saving or administrative convenience. That would empty the Directive of much of its effectiveness.

The better reading, consistent with CJEU case law on other discrimination directives, is:

- The worker must show that the fact of working part‑time is a ground on which they are treated less favourably than a comparable full‑timer (i.e. a “because of” test).  
- The employer is then permitted to justify that difference by “objective grounds” (the *Bilka‑Kaufhaus* style test: legitimate aim, appropriateness, necessity/proportionality).

The “solely because” language is doing essentially the same work as “on the ground of” in UK legislation, with mixed motives then addressed at the justification stage.

(c) The PTW Regs themselves  

Reg 5(2)(a) imports the same “on the ground that” formula used in other discrimination contexts. There is no textual indication that “sole reason” is required, and reading such a requirement in would make the protection markedly weaker than other discrimination protections and weaker than the EU measure it implements.

An English appellate court would very likely:

- Align reg 5(2)(a) with the *Nagarajan* approach: the part‑time status must be a real and effective cause of the less favourable treatment, but need not be the only reason.  
- Treat the employer’s business justifications as belonging under reg 5(2)(b) (objective justification), not as defeating causation at the threshold.

Accordingly, Avalon Reeves does **not** have to show that his part‑time status was the sole reason for the treatment; it is enough that it was one effective, significant reason.

---

3. Does the “circuit fee” amount to less favourable treatment “on the ground” of part‑time status?  

(a) Existence of a comparator and less favourable treatment  

- Comparable full‑time workers exist: other Stone Rides drivers doing the same work under the same type of contract.
- Formally, all drivers pay the same flat “circuit fee”. But under the PTW framework, tribunals look at substance, not just form.

Because the fee is fixed, a part‑timer who works fewer hours bears a higher cost per hour worked (and per pound earned) than a full‑timer:

- Suppose both earn £X per hour, but all pay £F per week for the circuit.  
- Net hourly return for a full‑timer (many hours) is significantly higher than for a part‑timer once the fixed fee is deducted.

That is structurally the same type of problem addressed by the pro‑rata temporis principle: employment‑related advantages and burdens that are tied to hours should, where appropriate, be adjusted proportionally, absent objective justification. The fact that a contractual term is facially uniform does not prevent it being “less favourable” in its economic effect on part‑timers.

Cases such as *British Airways plc v Pinaud* show that tribunals can and should look at the real economic advantage/disadvantage to the part‑timer, not just at whether the literal wording of the term is identical.

On that analysis, Reeves is “treated … less favourably” as regards his remuneration/financial terms when compared with a full‑time driver.

(b) Causation: is that “on the ground that” he is part‑time?  

Both sides accept his part‑time status is a factor in the treatment.

- But for the fact that workers like Reeves work fewer hours, the flat fee would not operate in a more onerous way for them. Their disadvantage arises specifically from the interaction between the fee and the reduced hours of part‑time work.
- That connection between being part‑time and being worse‑off in pay‑related terms is enough to satisfy “on the ground that” under a *Nagarajan*‑style, “one effective cause” test.

Stone Rides’ argument that the principal motive is “revenue generation” does not negate that the worker’s part‑time status is an effective cause of the comparative disadvantage. Business aims and sector norms may be relevant to justification; they do not convert what is in substance a part‑time‑linked detriment into something else at the causation stage.

An English court, applying the usual discrimination analysis, would therefore be likely to find that reg 5(2)(a) is met: the less favourable treatment is “on the ground that” Reeves works part‑time, even if there are also commercial motives.

---

4. Objective justification  

Once less favourable treatment on the ground of part‑time status is established, the burden shifts to the employer to justify it on objective grounds.

Stone Rides’ justifications:

- Funding the booking system and commercial viability.  
- Administrative difficulty/unworkability of pro‑rating fixed business costs.  
- Alignment with sector practice.

These can be legitimate aims in principle, but the employer must also show that the means chosen are appropriate and necessary, and that less discriminatory alternatives are not reasonably available.

On the limited facts given:

- Stone Rides has not shown why a fee structure that is more closely tied to use (e.g. percentage commission per booking, or fees scaled by contracted hours or volume) would not serve the same revenue aim with less disproportionate impact on part‑timers.
- “Sector norms” and general administrative convenience, without evidence of real difficulty or disproportionate burden in adopting a less discriminatory model, are usually insufficient to discharge the justification burden.
- The flat fee is a crude mechanism that predictably and significantly disadvantages part‑timers relative to full‑timers in terms of net hourly earnings, and there is no indication of serious exploration of alternatives.

On those facts, a tribunal properly applying the “objective justification” test would be unlikely to find the treatment justified.

---

5. Conclusion  

- As a matter of law, “on the ground that” in reg 5(2)(a) should not be read as imposing a “sole reason” test. It is enough that part‑time status is one effective cause of the treatment.  
- Applying that interpretation, Reeves’ part‑time status is plainly linked to the greater burden of the circuit fee; that satisfies the causation requirement.  
- Stone Rides’ business reasons are for the justification stage and, on the information available, do not amount to a robust objective justification for imposing a flat fee that disproportionately burdens part‑time workers.

Accordingly, an English court should find that Reeves has suffered unlawful less favourable treatment under the PTW Regs, and his claim should succeed.

Under the Federal Arbitration Act (FAA), whether a nonsignatory can compel arbitration is governed by ordinary state-law principles of contract and agency, as incorporated into federal arbitration doctrine. Courts recognize several theories under which a nonsignatory may enforce (or be bound by) an arbitration agreement, including: (1) agency; (2) veil-piercing/alter ego; (3) successor/assumption; (4) third‑party beneficiary; and (5) equitable estoppel (including “intertwined claims” / “direct-benefit estoppel”). The federal policy favoring arbitration applies strongly to questions of scope, but not to whether an agreement exists; that latter issue is governed by state contract principles.

Here, the question is whether Jon Davidson, who did not personally sign the original investment contract, can compel Harper Investors to arbitrate their claims against him under a clause covering “any controversies arising out of or relating to” the agreement with Gold Reserve & Lending.

I. Agency / Officer–Employee Theory

Many federal courts have held that corporate officers, directors, and employees of a signatory can invoke that entity’s arbitration clause for claims based on conduct within the scope of their corporate roles:

- E.g., Letizia v. Prudential Bache Sec., Inc. (9th Cir.) and Pritzker v. Merrill Lynch (3d Cir.) allow employees and agents of a signatory broker-dealer to compel arbitration where the employer’s agreement with the customer contains an arbitration provision and the claims against the individuals are factually intertwined with claims against the firm.

The rationale: (1) the corporation can only act through its officers/agents; and (2) a plaintiff cannot circumvent an arbitration agreement with the company merely by suing individuals for the same conduct.

On the facts:

- Davidson became the owner (through National Freight Consolidated), officer, and director of Gold Reserve & Lending.
- The alleged misconduct—relating to the tax shelter / container-leasing program and ongoing dealings with Harper after they invested—grew out of that business relationship.
- To the extent Harper’s claims are premised on how the tax shelter investment was marketed, administered, or “fixed,” and on how Davidson, as the person in control of the signatory company, handled those matters, he is being sued for conduct taken in his corporate role.

Under standard agency principles, if Gold Reserve & Lending (the signatory) can compel arbitration for those disputes, its controlling officer can ordinarily do the same when sued personally for the same underlying conduct. Harper Investors’ consent to arbitrate “any controversies” regarding the investment agreement with the company reasonably encompasses disputes over actions taken by the company’s officers when acting in that capacity.

II. Successor / Ownership and Corporate Separateness

Davidson acquired Gold Reserve & Lending via National Freight Consolidated and then operated it. The corporate entity that signed the contract remained the same; its ownership changed. Contract obligations and rights—including the arbitration clause—continue with the entity regardless of who owns its stock.

Thus, as a matter of corporate law:

- Gold Reserve & Lending retains the right to enforce the arbitration clause.
- Davidson, as its officer and controlling owner, stands in a standard agent/principal relationship to the entity.

Harper emphasizes that Davidson also used distinct entities (Universal Business Services, Fund Restoration Alliance, Tax Support Circle) with no formal connection to the original contract and that he maintained corporate separateness when convenient. That cuts both ways:

- If Harper’s theory is that these entities and Davidson were effectively working in concert with Gold Reserve & Lending as part of one scheme, that closeness supports treating Davidson as sufficiently identified with the signatory to invoke its arbitration clause (agency / alter-ego flavor).
- If, instead, these acts were truly independent ventures, unrelated to the original investment contract, that might undercut his ability to rely on the original clause—but then the question becomes one of *scope* (see below), not formal privity.

Courts typically do not let a plaintiff have it both ways: you cannot plead a unified, concerted fraudulent enterprise built around the original investment relationship to expand liability to a nonsignatory individual, yet deny that same individual the benefit of the arbitration clause that governs disputes about that very relationship.

III. Equitable Estoppel / “Intertwined Claims”

Equitable estoppel is a major route for nonsignatories to compel arbitration. Two common formulations:

1. A nonsignatory can compel arbitration when the signatory’s claims are “intertwined” with the underlying contract containing the arbitration clause and allege “substantially interdependent and concerted misconduct” by the nonsignatory and the signatory.

2. A signatory is estopped from avoiding arbitration when it directly benefits from a contract (or sues on that contract), yet seeks to avoid the arbitration clause in that same contract when sued by someone closely tied to it.

Applying that here:

- The core dispute arises out of the same tax shelter investment Harper purchased under the contract with Gold Reserve & Lending.
- Harper’s allegations portray Davidson as a central actor in the same broader scheme as Gold Reserve & Lending—initial investment, tax shelter structure, and subsequent dealings “in connection with the container leasing program.”
- The factual allegations against Davidson and against the original contracting entity are clearly interdependent and arise from the same transactional nucleus.

That is exactly the sort of situation in which federal courts use equitable estoppel to permit a nonsignatory individual (officer/owner) to enforce an arbitration clause, so that a plaintiff cannot rely on the contract and its relationship for liability while disavowing its dispute-resolution mechanism.

IV. Scope of the Arbitration Clause

The clause covers controversies “arising out of or relating to” the investment agreement. Courts interpret “relating to” broadly. Even tort claims—fraud, misrepresentation, breach of fiduciary duty—are typically arbitrable when:

- They originate from the parties’ contractual relationship;
- They concern performance, administration, or unwinding of the contract; or
- They would not exist “but for” the contractual relationship, and resolution will substantially involve facts and rights created by that agreement.

Harper argues that:

- Some of Davidson’s alleged misconduct (e.g., forming Fund Restoration Alliance and Tax Support Circle to solicit additional funds, advising investors not to pursue certain suits) occurred after the original contract and via separate entities;
- These acts are independent torts, not contract-related.

But the nature of those claims still appears tied to the investment relationship:

- Davidson’s solicitations and “help” were aimed at investors in the tax shelter program born out of the original contract.
- His alleged discouragement of lawsuits and promises of assistance were in the context of dealing with problems arising from that same investment.
- These are not random, unrelated wrongs; they are derivative of, and responsive to, the original investment and its fallout.

Under the generous “relating to” standard, courts almost always treat such downstream fraud and “cleanup” schemes as sufficiently related to the original investment agreement to fall within an arbitration clause, particularly in financial and tax shelter contexts. Resolving these claims will inevitably involve examining the rights and obligations created by the original contract, how the investment was supposed to work, and what the parties expected.

On balance, the post-contract timing and use of additional entities do not detach these claims so far from the original agreement as to take them outside the “relating to” language.

V. Harper’s Consent Argument and Non‑Signatory Status

Harper is correct that arbitration is fundamentally consensual, and the FAA does not let a stranger impose arbitration where there was no agreement. But in mainstream U.S. arbitration doctrine:

- Consent is not limited to literal signatures; it includes consent flowing through agency, corporate structure, and equitable estoppel where the plaintiff’s own conduct and claims tether the nonsignatory to the contract.
- When a party signs a broad arbitration clause with a company and later sues that company’s officers and owners for their roles in the same business relationship, courts have repeatedly found that the signatory has, as a practical and legal matter, agreed that those related disputes will go to arbitration.

Thus, the argument that Harper “never agreed to arbitrate with Davidson personally” has force only if Davidson’s role and the claims against him are genuinely collateral to the contractual relationship. The facts given suggest the opposite: their relationship with Davidson arises precisely because of, and is centered on, that investment.

VI. Default / Waiver

Harper points to the entry of default against Davidson and argues he should not be permitted to “game” the system.

Under Rule 55 and FAA principles:

- An entry of default (as opposed to a final default judgment) can be set aside for “good cause.”
- Waiver of the right to arbitration typically requires (1) knowing participation in litigation inconsistent with arbitration, and (2) prejudice to the other side (e.g., extensive discovery, motions practice, delay).

Here, Davidson “simultaneously” sought to compel arbitration while a default was entered. That timing suggests:

- Minimal litigation activity by Davidson inconsistent with arbitration;
- Limited, if any, prejudice to Harper beyond what is inherent in moving from court to arbitration.

Given the strong federal policy favoring arbitration, courts are generally willing to set aside a procedural default and allow arbitration where a valid arbitration right exists and the defendant has not substantially litigated on the merits. A mere failure to answer before moving to compel—without more—usually does not constitute a knowing, prejudicial waiver.

Equitable “gamesmanship” concerns are real, but on these facts, the scale of prejudice to Harper from vacating the default and compelling arbitration is comparatively modest, particularly since the dispute is already framed as one covered by an arbitration clause.

VII. Overall Assessment

Putting everything together:

- Davidson was the owner/officer/director of the signatory company and dealt with Harper in that capacity concerning the same investment contract and its fallout.
- The claims against him are tightly intertwined with the contract containing the arbitration clause and with the alleged conduct of the signatory entity.
- Agency and equitable-estoppel doctrines, as applied under the FAA and state contract law in most jurisdictions, generally allow such a nonsignatory officer to compel arbitration to prevent end-runs around a bargained-for arbitration clause.
- The broad “arising out of or relating to” language readily encompasses the fraud and post-contract misconduct alleged here, given their direct connection to the tax shelter investment.
- The presence of an entry of default, without substantial litigation or demonstrated prejudice, is not enough to defeat the arbitration right.

On these facts and under prevailing arbitration jurisprudence, a U.S. court is more likely to permit Davidson to compel arbitration despite his nonsignatory status.

1. Statutory framework and questions

A charitable remainder passing from a decedent’s estate is deductible only if:

1. Under § 2055(a) and the regulations, the value of the charitable remainder is “presently ascertainable” and thus severable from the noncharitable interest at the date of death; and  
2. Where there is a split‑interest trust (private life interest + charitable remainder), § 2055(e)(2) further requires that the charitable remainder be in an approved form (CRAT, CRUT, or pooled income fund), unless the trust can be brought within § 2055(e)(3)’s reformation provisions.

So there are two core questions:

- Is the charitable remainder “presently ascertainable” under § 2055(a)?  
- Even if it was not originally deductible, does § 2055(e)(3) allow the 1988 reformation to retroactively qualify the remainder for a deduction, in light of (a) the pre‑1979 execution requirement and (b) the need for a “reformable interest”?

2. Execution date: 1971 will vs. 1982 codicil

Section 2055(e)(3) gives special reformation relief to certain instruments “executed before” a particular cutoff (here, before January 1, 1979, under the facts as presented). The Government argues the 1982 codicil effectively re‑executes the will, pushing it past the cutoff.

a. How execution date should be treated

- Under traditional wills doctrine, a codicil republishes the will as of the date of the codicil; the will and codicil are read together as one testamentary instrument speaking from the codicil date.  
- Congress drew a line at instruments executed before a certain date to give relief to older estate plans that were put in place without full awareness of the later, detailed split‑interest rules; it did not intend perpetual “grandfathering” for documents that were substantially revised after those rules were well known.

Here, Mary Winston did more than a mere clerical correction. The codicils (including the 1982 codicil) “adjusted some details regarding Kevin Fletcher’s lifetime benefits.” Those are noncharitable interests that directly affect how much is left for Elmwood University. Revising the terms of the life estate changes the economic structure of the split interest.

Given:

- The statutory language focuses on the date the “will or trust” is executed, not on whether the charitable clause itself was altered;  
- The codicil modifies the basic economic arrangement between the life tenant and the remainder beneficiary; and  
- The core purpose of the cutoff is to deny special reformation relief to instruments that were actively maintained or revised after the rules were in place,

a court applying ordinary principles of will construction plus statutory purpose has strong reason to treat the governing instrument, as a whole, as executed on the date of the last codicil—in 1982.

b. Consequence

If the governing instrument is treated as executed in 1982, it is not within the class of pre‑1979 instruments eligible for § 2055(e)(3) reformation relief. On that basis alone, the 1988 reformation cannot bring the trust within § 2055(e)(3), and the charitable deduction fails.

Even if a court were inclined to be flexible about the execution‑date issue, the estate still faces a second, independent obstacle: the “presently ascertainable” requirement.

3. Presently ascertainable value of the remainder

To be deductible under § 2055(a), the charitable remainder must have a “presently ascertainable” value, determinable from the terms of the instrument and applicable state law as of the date of death. This requirement is longstanding and independent of § 2055(e)(2) and (e)(3).

The Supreme Court has drawn a line between:

- A power to invade principal constrained by an objective standard such as “support and maintenance in reasonable comfort,” which can be actuarially valued (Ithaca Trust), and  
- A broad or subjective invasion power (e.g., for “happiness,” “pleasure,” “comfort and welfare,” or similar open‑ended notions) that leaves the remainder effectively speculative (Henslee and its progeny).

a. Terms of Mary Winston’s trust

Kevin Fletcher is given:

- Fixed monthly financial payments (which are capable of valuation), and  
- In addition, a broad right to have the trust pay:

  - his medical expenses,  
  - his taxes,  
  - the upkeep and improvements of a residence in Riverside, and  
  - unspecified “other expenditures.”

The key features:

- “Improvements” to the residence are not limited to maintenance of an existing standard; they can constitute capital enhancements with no intrinsic ceiling. Money used for capital improvements of property that is not part of the charitable remainder is effectively a permanent depletion of the corpus vis‑à‑vis the charity.  
- The phrase “other expenditures” is an open‑ended catch‑all, not cabined by a standard such as “support” or “maintenance.”  
- The trustee’s power to invade is thus potentially very broad; nothing in the instrument, as summarized, imposes an enforceable objective standard that allows a court or the IRS to reliably bound the maximum potential invasion.

b. Impact on ascertainability

In determining deductibility, courts do not assume that the trustee will behave frugally or that the life tenant’s needs will be modest; rather, they must consider the full scope of what the trustee is empowered to do. If the trustee could—consistent with the instrument and state fiduciary law—consume the entire corpus for Kevin’s benefit (for example, by authorizing extensive improvements to the Riverside residence or broad “other expenditures”), then the charitable remainder is not “presently ascertainable” in the sense required for § 2055.

Fiduciary duties and the beneficiary’s age (Kevin being in his eighties) do not cure this, because:

- The question is what the governing instrument authorizes, not what seems probable in hindsight or based on subjective expectations; and  
- The Supreme Court has repeatedly rejected arguments that rely on presumed moderation by trustees or beneficiaries when the instrument grants broad, subjective invasion powers.

On these terms, the charitable remainder to Elmwood University is too uncertain in amount at the moment of Mary Winston’s death to qualify for a deduction under § 2055(a).

4. Does § 2055(e)(3) allow reformation of a non‑ascertainable remainder?

Even if a court were to accept Harper Bank’s position on the execution date and treat the will as “pre‑1979,” § 2055(e)(3) still does not rescue a remainder whose value was not presently ascertainable at death.

Section 2055(e)(3):

- Is explicitly aimed at curing failures to comply with the formal split‑interest rules of § 2055(e)(2) (e.g., converting a defective split‑interest into a CRAT or CRUT).  
- Presupposes that, absent the form defect, there is a charitable interest of the type otherwise allowable under § 2055(a).

In other words, to be a “reformable interest” the interest must fail solely because it is not in an approved form (annuity trust, unitrust, pooled fund, etc.), not because the underlying remainder’s value was inherently unascertainable at the outset.

Here, the trust does not merely fail the CRAT/CRUT structural requirements. The broader, more fundamental problem is that the trustee’s invasion powers for Kevin’s benefit make the value of Elmwood’s remainder speculative. That is a § 2055(a) problem, not simply a § 2055(e)(2) problem.

Allowing § 2055(e)(3) reformation in such a situation would:

- Convert a remainder that was effectively non‑deductible ab initio (because its value was not ascertainable) into a fully deductible CRAT‑type remainder by judicial fiat;  
- Create a deduction that was not tied, in any meaningful way, to what the charity was reasonably expected to receive when the decedent died; and  
- Undermine the statutory objective that the estate tax deduction approximate the value actually destined for charity.

Courts have consistently interpreted charitable deduction provisions strictly, in line with the principle that tax deductions are matters of legislative grace. Using § 2055(e)(3) to salvage a remainder whose value was never ascertainable in the first place pushes the statute beyond its corrective, technical‑fix function and into rewriting the underlying donative scheme.

5. Effect of the 1988 reformation

The 1988 state‑court reformation converting Kevin Fletcher’s interest to a fixed annual amount does align the trust *going forward* with the CRAT/CRUT model. But for federal estate tax purposes:

- The relevant valuation date is Mary Winston’s date of death in 1985.  
- A post‑death reformation can only have retroactive tax effect to the extent § 2055(e)(3) permits.  
- Because (1) the governing instrument is properly treated as executed after the statutory cutoff, and (2) the remainder was not a “reformable interest” due to lack of ascertainability, § 2055(e)(3) does not authorize retroactive correction here.

Thus, while the reformation may be effective under state law to govern post‑1988 distributions, it cannot retroactively create a federal estate tax charitable deduction that the statute otherwise denies.

6. Conclusion

Mary Winston clearly intended to benefit Elmwood University, and Harper Bank acted in good faith to bring the trust into technical compliance. But under the governing federal tax rules:

- The instrument, as ultimately executed via the 1982 codicil, falls outside the class of pre‑cutoff instruments eligible for § 2055(e)(3) reformation; and  
- Independently, the broad, discretionary power to expend principal for “upkeep and improvements” and “other expenditures” for Kevin Fletcher renders Elmwood’s remainder not “presently ascertainable” at death, and thus not a “reformable interest” under § 2055(e)(3).

For these reasons, a court applying the statute and relevant precedent should deny the estate tax charitable deduction and rule for the Government.
